##Q4

## Research question
 
Do party type, court level, and year predict whether an AI hallucination incident involved completely fabricated case law?
 
```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(randomForest)
 
ai_raw <- read_csv("hallucination_cases.csv")
ai_clean <- ai_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(`Hallucination Items`), !is.na(`Party(ies)`), !is.na(Court), !is.na(Date)) |>
  mutate(
    is_fabricated_case = factor(ifelse(str_detect(`Hallucination Items`, "Fabricated: Case Law"), "Yes", "No")),
    party_binary = case_when(
      `Party(ies)` == "Lawyer" ~ "Lawyer",
      `Party(ies)` == "Pro Se Litigant" ~ "Pro Se Litigant",
      TRUE ~ "Other"),
    court_level = ifelse(str_detect(Court, "D\\.|Cir|USA"), "Federal", "State/Tribunal"),
    Year = as.integer(format(Date, "%Y"))
  ) |>
  filter(party_binary != "Other") |>
  mutate(across(c(party_binary, court_level), as.factor)) |>
  select(is_fabricated_case, party_binary, court_level, Year)
 
set.seed(154)
train_id <- sample(1:nrow(ai_clean), round(0.8 * nrow(ai_clean)))
ai_train <- ai_clean[train_id, ]
ai_test <- ai_clean[-train_id, ]
```
 
## Exploratory analysis
 
```{r}
ggplot(ai_clean, aes(x = party_binary, fill = is_fabricated_case)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  facet_wrap(~ court_level) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "yellow")) +
  labs(title = "Fabricated Case Law by Party Type and Court Level",
       x = "Party Type", y = "Proportion", fill = "Fabricated Case Law") +
  theme_minimal()
```
 
```{r}
ai_clean |> group_by(party_binary, court_level) |>
  summarise(n = n(), prop_fabricated = mean(is_fabricated_case == "Yes"), .groups = "drop")
```
 
## Decision tree
 
```{r}
tree_fit <- rpart(is_fabricated_case ~ ., data = ai_train, method = "class",
                  parms = list(split = "gini"))
tree_fit
```
 
Even with the default settings, the tree makes no splits and every leaf still predicts "Yes." To see what structure there is, we force a depth-2 tree (`cp = -1`).
 
```{r}
tree_big <- rpart(is_fabricated_case ~ ., data = ai_train, method = "class",
                  parms = list(split = "gini"),
                  control = rpart.control(cp = -1, maxdepth = 2))
rpart.plot(tree_big)
```
 
Cases from 2026 have a lower rate of fabricated case law (80%) than earlier cases (86%). Within 2026, lawyers' filings have fabricated case law less often (74%) than pro se filings (84%). Before 2026, federal and state courts look almost the same. Every leaf still predicts "Yes," so the tree shows differences in probability, not different predictions.
 
## Random forest
 
```{r}
set.seed(154)
rf_fit <- randomForest(is_fabricated_case ~ ., data = ai_train, ntree = 500)
rf_fit
```
 
## Comparing the models
 
```{r}
tree_pred <- predict(tree_fit, ai_test, type = "class")
rf_pred <- predict(rf_fit, ai_test)
c(baseline = mean(ai_test$is_fabricated_case == "Yes"),
  tree = mean(tree_pred == ai_test$is_fabricated_case),
  forest = mean(rf_pred == ai_test$is_fabricated_case))
table(Forest = rf_pred, Actual = ai_test$is_fabricated_case)
```
 
The random forest also predicts "Yes" for every case. Its out-of-bag error, 17.4%, is just the share of "No" cases. The tree, the forest, and the baseline of always predicting "Yes" all have the same test accuracy. Neither model adds predictive value, but the forest is harder to interpret.
 
## Conclusions and limitations
 
Fabricated case law appears in about 83% of cases regardless of party type or court level. Pro se filings have it somewhat more often than lawyers' filings (84–86% vs. 78–81%), and the rate dipped in 2026. These differences are too small to change any prediction, so a model with these predictors cannot beat simply guessing "fabricated."
 
As far as limitations go, the outcome is built by string matching, same as last. Also, the database only includes publicly reported cases where hallucinations were caught, so it is not a true random sample.
